title: Obsession Cost Less Than a Bollywood Song Shoot. It Just Crossed $224 Million.
excerpt: The $750K horror film with a 26-year-old first-time director has left Spielberg shaken, Indian multiplexes packed, and everyone asking how a supernatural toy became the year's most terrifying weapon.
body:
There are box office success stories, and then there is **Obsession**.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=gMC8kkwbIQQ</youtube>

A supernatural horror film made for $750,000 — roughly what **Cocktail 2** spent on its Sicily song shoot — has just crossed $224 million worldwide. In India, it pulled ₹42.60 crore in ten days, with a second weekend that was 125% bigger than its first. That number isn't a typo. The film literally got *more* popular after everyone had already seen it.

Welcome to the most improbable hit of the decade.

**Curry Barker** — 26 years old, first-time director, zero industry pedigree — made Obsession with a micro-budget, a supernatural toy called the One Wish Willow, and a cast of relative unknowns. **Michael Johnston** plays Bear, a lonely music store employee still carrying a torch for his childhood crush Nikki, played by **Inde Navarrette**. One night, Bear breaks the Willow and makes a single wish: he wants Nikki to love him. She does. Immediately. Completely. Terrifyingly.

> "I have seen Obsession, and I loved it." — Steven Spielberg

What follows is a slow-burn descent into genuine dread. Obsession doesn't rely on jump scares or gore — it earns its horror through atmosphere, through the creeping realization that getting exactly what you wished for might be the worst thing that ever happens to you. Bear wanted love. What he got was possession wearing love's face. Think **Monkey's Paw** meets **Fatal Attraction**, directed by someone who understood that the scariest thing on screen isn't a monster — it's a person looking at you with too much love in their eyes.

The Indian audience has turned this into a full-blown cultural event. The film opened to a modest ₹1.60 crore on Day 1 in Indian theatres. By its second Saturday, it was pulling ₹8 crore in a single day — five times its opening. Multiplexes across Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru reported packed evening shows. On its second Sunday, it collected ₹8.75 crore, wrapping the weekend at ₹20.75 crore — nearly matching its entire first-week haul of ₹22 crore.

Trade analysts are calling it "unheard of." A Hollywood horror film posting a 125% jump in its second weekend in India? That simply doesn't happen. Horror titles are supposed to be front-loaded, burning through their audience in the first five days and disappearing into the OTT void. Obsession is doing the opposite — growing week after week, driven by the kind of word-of-mouth that no marketing budget can manufacture.

The global numbers tell the same story. The film debuted at No. 3 at the US box office, then climbed its way into **Focus Features**' all-time Top 5. At $224 million against a $750K budget, it has earned more than 290 times its production cost. If it crosses the $207 million domestic mark currently held by Steven Soderbergh's **Traffic**, it becomes Focus Features' biggest release ever. Spielberg publicly praised the film — a rare stamp from someone who knows a thing or two about keeping audiences in their seats. The comparison isn't accidental: the last time a film defied its second-weekend trajectory this dramatically outside the holiday season was Spielberg's own **E.T.** in 1982.

For diaspora audiences, this is the easiest recommendation of the summer. Obsession is playing widely across the US, UK, Canada, and Australia in English. No subtitle hunting, no figuring out which OTT service has the rights in your country, no niche password sharing. Walk into any multiplex this week and experience the most talked-about film of 2026. At 108 minutes, it won't even wreck your dinner plans.

Produced by **Blumhouse Productions** — the house that built **Get Out**, **M3GAN**, and **The Black Phone** — the film carries a 95% critics' score and 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, with an 8.1 on IMDb and an A- CinemaScore. Its strength isn't in franchise recognition or star power. It's in something older and rarer: a genuinely original story, a concept that crawls under your skin and refuses to leave.

Barker — a filmmaker younger than half the producers who passed on his script — has made himself impossible to ignore. He's the definition of what happens when raw talent meets the right material and the industry gets out of the way.

If you haven't seen it yet, stop scrolling and book a ticket. The One Wish Willow is waiting.

**Obsession** is now playing in theatres across India and worldwide.
author: Diaspora Desk
